title: Physical Fitness From Ancient Greece to Modern Times
sourceTitle: History of physical training and fitness

pages.text:
People have trained their bodies for a long time. They want good health and strong skills. In old Greece, men ran and lifted big stones. Later, Roman rulers stopped the early games.

Soon, training became mostly for soldiers.
pages.caption: Roman relief of a legionary, 2nd century AD

evidence.articleCaption: Ancient Roman relief showing a legionary. Antikensammlung, 2nd century AD

pages.text: Old Greeks played a fun team game called Epikoinos. The ball was about the size of a large apple. Two teams stood on opposite sides of a stone line in a staggered way. Players hit a small ball with their hands. Each team tried to push the ball past the other side's goal line.
pages.caption: 76kg stone throw from Greek tradition

pages.text: In old Rome, people enjoyed active ball games too. Soldiers also trained hard every day. One game was called Trigon. Three players stood at the three points of a triangle and threw or hit a ball very fast to each other. They used their hands to hit the ball back and forth quickly.
pages.caption: Roman sarcophagus battle scene, c. 190 AD

evidence.articleCaption: This battle scene found on a Roman sarcophagus demonstrates the excellent physical conditioning of both Roman soldiers and Celtic warriors. Dallas Museum of Art, c. 190 AD.

pages.text: In South Asia, body training was linked to faith and war. Some experts study very old art from the Indus Valley. They ask if those figures show early yoga poses. In China, people kept their own ways to stay strong for a long time. Later, leaders began to support Western sports and modern games too.

Across history, most people wanted a strong and healthy body. Men and women often followed different training plans. Culture and body needs shaped these plans. In many places, women did light moves for quick steps and good form. Men often trained more for heavy work, long runs, and hard fights.

pages.text: Humans have practiced physical training for centuries to improve health, skill, and competition. Ancient Greeks ran, wrestled, and lifted heavy stones. After Rome banned the early Olympics, exercise shifted toward military duty.

pages.text: Ancient Romans combined active games with strict training for their soldiers. A popular game called Trigon placed three players at the corners of a triangle. They tossed and struck a ball rapidly between teammates using their hands very quickly.
pages.caption: Roman sarcophagus battle relief, c. 190 AD

evidence.articleCaption: This battle scene found on a Roman sarcophagus demonstrates the excellent physical conditioning of both Roman soldiers and Celtic warriors. Dallas Museum of Art, c. 190 AD.

pages.text: In South Asia, physical training connected closely to religious practice. Historians still debate whether ancient Indus Valley carvings depict early yoga postures. Meanwhile, China maintained its distinct athletic traditions. Later governments promoted Western sports.

Throughout history, fitness routines aimed for balanced strength and health rather than extreme size. Men and women followed separate exercises.

Women's traditional routines focused on grace, agility, and upright posture rather than heavy endurance.

C1-C2.headline: The Evolution of Human Conditioning and Exercise

pages.text: Organized conditioning historically served athletic rivalry, physiological resilience, and aesthetic ideals. Following the Roman prohibition of Hellenic Olympic festivals, systematic exercise increasingly prioritized martial utility.
pages.caption: Roman legionary relief, 2nd century AD

evidence.articleCaption: Ancient Roman relief showing a legionary. Antikensammlung, 2nd century AD

pages.text:
Classical Greek athletics included Epikoinos, an energetic territorial ball contest contested across a central gypsum demarcation.

Equally matched formations maneuvered in staggered ranks to propel the sphere past rival boundaries.
pages.caption: Stone-throwing tradition from Ancient Greece

pages.text:
Roman physical culture paired rigorous legionary conditioning with brisk recreational pastimes.

In Trigon, three participants positioned at triangular vertices exchanged rapid throws and strikes demanding sharp reflexes and coordination.
pages.caption: Roman sarcophagus battle scene, c. 190 AD

evidence.articleCaption: This battle scene found on a Roman sarcophagus demonstrates the excellent physical conditioning of both Roman soldiers and Celtic warriors. Dallas Museum of Art, c. 190 AD.

pages.text: Across South Asia, somatic discipline intersected with spiritual devotion, fueling debate over whether Indus Valley artifacts depict early yogic postures. China sustained autonomous athletic traditions before modern administrations institutionalized sports.

Historical conditioning philosophies cultivated anatomical harmony rather than excessive bulk. Divergent regimens reflected physiological distinctions. Feminine exercise frameworks prioritized kinetic agility, poise, and postural alignment over heavy endurance.

Humans have practiced physical training for centuries to improve health, skill, and competition. Ancient Greeks ran, wrestled, and lifted heavy stones. After Rome banned the early Olympics, exercise shifted toward military duty.
